newsitem.title: UK: Major to step up attack on EU social chapter.
newsitem.headline: Major to step up attack on EU social chapter.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major is preparing to launch his fiercest attack yet on what he sees as over-regulation in Europe in an attempt to highlight policy differences with Labour leader Tony Blair.

Major is scheduled to give a keynote speech to businessmen in Brussels on Tuesday that aides said would denounce the European Union's social chapter on workplace standards as a recipe for job destruction.
"Over-regulation doesn't work, and as a result nor do millions of Europeans," Major is expected to say.
Labour, the main opposition party, has pledged to sign the social chapter if, as opinion polls suggest, it wins Britain's looming election.

Major, whose government has opted out of the social chapter, believes he can capitalise on one of the clearest policy differences between Labour and his Conservative party to warn voters that a Blair administration would derail Britain's economic recovery.

Hardly any legislation has been introduced so far under the umbrella of the social chapter, but Major's ministers insist that the European Commission, the EU's Brussels-based executive, has plenty of onerous laws up its sleeve that would shackle British business.
"If we sign the social chapter it will become a Trojan horse unloading on Britain all the problems that brought us two our knees in the 1970s," Major will say.
Aides said the prime minister would argue that Europe, with unemployment rates far higher than those in Britain or the United States, was at a turning point.
"Crudely the choice is between two dramatically different economic philosophies -- the enterprise approach and the social model," he is expected to say.

Major believes that continental Europe has a lot to learn from Britain's success in making its labour market more flexible by curbing the power of unions, relaxing hiring-and-firing rules and keeping non-wage costs on employers low.
Whereas non-wage costs add just 15 percent to the salary bill in Britain, they reach 31 percent in Germany, 41 percent in France and 44 percent in Italy.
The European model of generous workplace perks and excessive regulation is "fundamentally flawed," Major concludes.
Labour was wrong to think it could just back away from aspects of social chapter legislation to which it objected.

"It is not some mail-order mistake you can send back if you don't like it. Britain would be powerless to stop our businesses being burdened with all kinds of unnecessary regulations," Major will warn.
Major's message builds on an advertising campaign his Conservatives launched on Monday depicting a weeping British lion and warning voters of "New Labour Euro Danger".
